old_title: Trump warns 'economic consequences' for nations helping Iran
new_title: Trump warns 'economic consequences' for nations helping Iran
old_text:
What you need to know
- US President Donald Trump announced the "most crushing economic operation" ever against Iran
- Trump said any country providing "any type of lifeline to Iran" will face "tremendous" economic repercussions
- Iran's media dismissed Trump's threat
Here are the latest developments from the Iran war and the Middle East on Thursday, August 20:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Australia 'outraged' over Israel declining to open criminal probe in World Central Kitchen deaths
Australia on Thursday summoned Israel's ambassador to protest a decision by its military to not launch criminal investigations into the death of an Australian aid worker during a 2024 Israeli air strike on Gaza.
Australian national Lalzawmi "Zomi" Frankcom was among a group of seven World Central Kitchen employees killed on April 1, 2024 when their aid convoy was hit in an Israeli strike.
The attack had drawn widespread international condemnation.
On Wednesday, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) said it had found no basis to probe the deaths of the charity's staff after a fact-finding and assessment procedure.
The IDF said in its report that it had mistakenly identified several individuals in the vehicles as Hamas militants and that the convoy deviated from its planned route. It concluded that "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who summoned Israeli ambassador Hillel Newman, said relations with Israel were "difficult" after the decision.
"This decision falls far short of the accountability we expect," Wong said, adding that Canberra was outraged.
Wong deemed Israel's move to not launch criminal proceedings into Frankcom and her colleagues' death as "especially insulting and hurtful" as it was announced on World Humanitarian Day.
"We do not have confidence" in Israel's investigation into the killings, she said. "The Australian government will continue to keep pressing Israel for justice."
Meanwhile, Newman after meeting Wong expressed "deep sorrow and grief" to Frankcom's family as he spoke to the media.
"Israel had no intention to attack or injure in any way the aid workers that were on the convoy," he stressed.
He said that Israel's decision was that there was no "criminal liability" and went on to say: "We must respect that conclusion."
Trump threatens Iran partners with economic punishment
US President Donald Trump has warned any country that supports Iran of economic consequences as war soon approaches its sixth month with no resolution in sight.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform on Wednesday that "ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS economic consequences."
The US leader described his move as "economic warfare" and "isolation" on an unprecedented scale as he stepped up an economic pressure campaign on Iran.
"Today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!" he said, referring to the Islamic Republic in the superlatives-embellished post.
Trump said that nobody other than him had given Tehran what he called "a greater opportunity to make a deal".
"TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it," he said.
Trump said that Washington needed the support of all its allies to isolate Iran and counter the threat posed by the country.
He compared his plan to an "ECONOMIC D-DAY".
There were no details of what Trump's economic steps against nations supporting Iran would look like, Trump also did not mention any country by name, other than Iran.
Iran media reacts to Trump's "economic warfare" warning
Iran's Fars news agency on Thursday called Trump's latest economic threat the usual "psychological warfare and propaganda campaign,"
The country's Tasnim news agency said the US presidents' announcement was "not a new development, as the United States has been trying for years to block any financial and economic ties with Iran."
Tehran has "learned how to circumvent these restrictions and has become very skilled at doing so," Tasnim said on Telegram.
Welcome to our coverage
Thank you for joining us as we bring you the latest edition of our rolling updates on the war in Iran and the wider Middle Eastern crisis.
But first here is a wrap up of the developments that took place in the region this week:
- US President Donald Trump emphasized that no talks or conversations between Washington and Tehran were being held
- The United Arab Emirates suspended trade ties with Iran after accusing the country of firing two ballistic missiles
- Human Rights Watch urged the United Nations to keep its international peacekeeping force in Lebanon, saying that a decision to end UNIFIL's mandate came before this year's war and the subsequent Israeli invasion of southern Lebanon
- The Israeli military announced criminal probes into two high-profile attacks during the Gaza war - the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in 2024 and 15 Palestinian paramedics in 2025
Follow along for more.

- Trump hs said any country providing "any type of lifeline to Iran" will face "tremendous" economic repercussions
- Iran's media has dismissed Trump's threat
- US sanctions on Iran are "economic terrorism," Tehran has said

US Treasury sanctions 10 individuals for alleged cash smuggling for Hezbollah
The United States Treasury on Thursday put sanctions on 10 individuals it accuses of involvement in smuggling networks for Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
"[Hezbollah] and its allies exploit financing schemes including oil smuggling, illicit shipping, commodities sales, and bulk cash smuggling to generate and move funds across the region," the Treasury said in its statement.
Among those targeted is a Turkish businessman the Treasury accuses of using Turkey-base exchange houses to move cash between other countries in the region and Hezbollah's base in Lebanon.
Washington also redesignated Hezbollah as a terrorist organization, citing "service to the Iranian regime under the command of Iran's [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) - Quds Force]"
The Quds Force is an elite unit of the IRGC in charge of its overseas operations. Earlier this year, the EU designated Iran's Revolutionary Guard a terror group.
US: Economic isolation will 'collapse' regime in Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Thursday that Washington believed economic pressure would successfully bring about regime change in Iran.
"It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this regime," Bessent told US broadcaster CNBC.
He said that the US would work to isolate Iran economically.
"This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world. And we are going to them and saying you are either with us or against us," he said.
He said that the strong economic pressure would make "large-scale" military operations unnecessary.
"If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart, but I will emphasize that is for no," he said.
Asked whether the United States would also pressure China to join in the drive to isolate Iran, he said "many conversations are best to have in private."
Iran's Foreign Ministry condemns new US sanctions as 'economic terrorism'
Iran's Foreign Ministry strongly condemned new US economic and trade sanctions on Thursday.
The ministry said that the measures amount to "economic terrorism" and crimes against humanity, adding that the sanctions will hurt ordinary Iranians.
"Sanctions and economic pressure are the other side of the coin of war and military aggression," the ministry said in its statement.
It comes after US President Donald Trump threatened "tremendous economc consequences" for "any country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran."
Iran executes Afghan national over January protests
Iran on Thursday executed an Afghan citizen convicted over the killing of police officers during anti-government protests in January.
The Mizan Online portal, which is tied to the Iranian judiciary, reported that Ghaem Hosseini was a foreign national without providing further details.
It said he was convicted of "of drawing a weapon and causing fear and terror, creating widespread insecurity, acting against people's physical integrity and national security in a manner that seriously disrupted public order."
The Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) group said that the 21-year-old was from neighboring Afghanistan and was hanged at Isfahan central prison.
IHR said that Hosseini was accused of kicking a policeman. It added that Iranian authorities had not presented evidence that Hosseini had carried out any acts that led to the death of police officers.
He is the fifth person to be hanged over the case involving the death of four police officers in Isfahan in central Iran in January.
He is the second Afghan national to be executed over the protests.
Iran is home to the largest Afghan diaspora population in the world, numbering over 4 million.
Dozens executed over protests
IHR says at least 28 people involved in the protest wave of December 2025 - January 2026 have been executed since March 19.
It said that hundreds of others have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty.
The mass protests in Iran began on 28 December 2025, with millions taking to the streets as demonstrations peaked in January.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) said at least 7,000 people were killed in the ensuing crackdown, some 6,500 of them protesters and 214 being security personnel.
Turkey, Egypt, Qatar call for compliance with Gaza ceasefire, condemn Israeli strikes
Turkey, Egypt and Qatar on Thursday condemned recent Israeli strikes on Gaza in a joint statement.
They called on the international community and the US-led Board of Peace to take necessary steps to ensure compliance with the ceasefire in the Palestinian enclave.
"The mediating countries underline that the intensification of Israeli attacks undermines regional and international efforts at a critical juncture," the statement read.
"The mediating countries stress the imperative for Israel to fully comply with all its obligations under the ceasefire agreement and to refrain from actions that could further undermine the ceasefire and escalate tensions," the three countries stressed.
"The mediating countries reiterate their call on the international community and the Board of Peace ... to take the necessary steps to ensure compliance with th ceasefire and to exert effective pressure to prevent further escalation."
What is the Board of Peace's plan for Gaza?
Last month, the Board of Peace said it had reached a deal for the complete disarmament of Hamas, classified by multiple countries as a terrorist organization, and other armed groups in Gaza.
The 15-point road map aimed at ending the war calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons.
Weeks later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel rejected the deal, calling instead for the "genuine" disarmament of Hamas before any Israeli withdrawal.
Qatar, Turkey and Egypt are all founding members of the 27-country Board of Peace, which was established by US President Donald Trump in January.
Vatican expresses 'serious concerns' about implementation of Israel-Lebanon deal
The Vatican expressed its concern on Thursday around the implementation of a US-brokered deal between Israel and Lebanon.
"The Holy See, whilst welcoming the signing of the document, has expressed serious concerns about the difficulties being encountered in implementing it, and has pledged its support for efforts to that end," the Vatican said.
The statement comes after Pope Leo XIV met with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the Vatican.
Aoun called on the Catholic Church to "support Lebanon's efforts to achieve a full Israeli withdrawal from the occupied Lebanese territories, paving the way for the reconstruction of what Israel has destroyed."
He also urged the Vatican to "continue their diplomatic efforts" to ensure Israel implements the terms of the US-brokered deal.
Lebanon's population is religiously diverse and has the largest concentration of Catholics in the Middle East, with members of the Maronite church particularly present in Beirut and parts of the country's northwest.
By convention, the post of Lebanon's president is filled by a Maronite Catholic.
What are the terms of the agreement between Lebanon and Israel?
The US-brokered framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon calls for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group and the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces, alongside the deployment of the Lebanese army.
As part of its military operations, Israel treats an area 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory as a "security zone." Under the terms of the agreement, Israel is to gradually hand back "pilot zones" in the area to Lebanon.
Hezbollah has denounced the agreement, calling it a threat to Lebanon's sovereignty.
Israel has continued to strike Lebanon and engage in demolition operations in its southern regions since the agreement was reached.
Israel warns Turkey against 'dangerous adventures in Syria'
Turkey says it will continue supporting Syria's sovereignty after Israel bombed a Syrian air base and accused Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of dragging his country into "dangerous adventures" there.
Armed gunmen seize tanker in Gulf of Aden off Yemen
Armed gunmen seized a tanker in the Gulf of Aden off Yemen, maritime security agencies said Thursday.
"The tanker has reportedly been boarded by six armed persons, who are now in control of the vessel and redirecting it towards Somalia," the European Union's Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) said.
United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) also reported the incident, saying that the tanker issued a distress call as it was approached 136 nautical miles east of Al Mukalla in Yemen.
UKMTO did not provide further details and did not say whether the tanker or it screw were safe.
Israelis begin moving into settlement evacuated in 2005
Israelis began moving into the settlement of Kadim in the occupied West Bank on Thursday, the Samaria Regional Council said.
The council is the administrative body that administers Israeli settlements in parts of the north of the occupied Palestinian territory. The area is home to some 50,000 Israeli settlers.
The council said that 30 families had moved into the reestablished settlement, hailing the move as a "historic milestone." They were accompanied by far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and regional council head Yossi Dagan.
"Twenty-one years after the crime of the expulsion from northern Samaria, today we have completed the rectification," Smotrich said, referring to the 2005 dismantlement of the settlement by Israeli authorities.
"These communities constitute a real security buffer for the entire state of Israel," he said.
He also vowed to establish another 19 settlements in the northern West Bank.
Smotrich himself lives in the settlement of Kedumim in the West Bank.
He also heads the Administration for Settlement Affairs, an agency that oversees settlement expansion and is part of the Defense Ministry.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.
Why did Israel evacuate West Bank settlements in 2005?
Kadim is one of four Israeli settlements - alongside Ganim, Sa-Nur and Homesh - in the northern West Bank that were evacuated by Israeli authorities under a 2005 unilateral disengagement plan.
The evacuation was largely carried out due to their isolation from major settlement blocs and proximity to densely populated Palestinian areas, including the major towns of Jenin and Nablus.
Kadim itself is located on a hilltop just 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) from Jenin.
The 2005 disengagement also included the evacuation of all 21 Israeli settlements in the Gaza Strip.
All four evacuated West Bank settlements have been reestablished by Israeli authorities over the course of 2025 and 2026.
Iran calls Trump's 'economic warfare' announcement 'diversion' from US domestic issues
Iran has slammed US President Donald Trump's "Economic D-Day" punishment plan against Tehran as a diversion from his country's economic problems.
"The so-called 'Economic D-Day' is a diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt and surging interest costs," Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X as he shared snippets of US media outlets reporting on the US gross national debt reaching $40 trillion.
He said Trump's latest announcement was a continuation of "failed policies".
"Doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat - and enmity of Iranians," Araghchi said.
The Iranian foreign minister added that "global economy and sovereignty worldwide" was threatened by what he called "US economic terrorism."
Britain denounces tender launch for Israeli E1 settlement in West Bank
The United Kingdom has summoned Israel's charge d'affaires in London as it condemned Israel's move to launch a tender for a controversial West Bank settlement project.
The plan would build 3,500 new apartments in an area known as E1, which lies between East Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim. The new development would effectively split the West Bank into two parts.
Late on Tuesday, Israel's Land Authority published a tender for the building of the first 1,234 housing units in the project.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on Wednesday called the move "an unacceptable and destructive act," saying that it would "endanger the viability of a two-state solution".
"I made clear to the Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar that the Israeli government must halt E1 plans immediately, retract the tender and stop all settlement expansion," Miliband said.
The UK, Germany, France and Italy had earlier cautioned companies against taking part in tenders for construction projects in the E1 and thereby engaging in "serious violations of international law."
